turns.assistant: Yes. Under California Civil Code 1950.5, the landlord has 21 days after you move out to return the deposit or send an itemized statement of any deductions. Take photos of the unit on move-out day and keep a copy of your lease and any move-in inspection report.

turns.user: what counts as normal wear and tear, they want to take 400 for painting
turns.assistant: Normal wear and tear is the gradual deterioration from ordinary use, like faded paint, worn carpet, small scuffs, and minor nail holes. Landlords generally can't charge for repainting after normal use, especially after a long tenancy, since paint has a usable life. Damage beyond ordinary use, like large holes, stains, or marks from pets or smoking, can be deducted. If they're charging for painting, ask them for the age of the paint and the specific damage that required it.

A large hole, or several holes that required patching, can be a legitimate deduction, but the landlord should show the cost of the repair. Ask for the itemized statement in writing and the actual invoice for any patching. If the charge for a few small holes is more than a patch and a touch-up would cost, push back and say so.

turns.user: what if they just never send anything after 21 days
turns.assistant: If the landlord misses the 21-day deadline, you can send a written demand letter asking for the full deposit back and noting that the deadline has passed. Under 1950.5, a landlord who keeps a deposit in bad faith can be liable for up to twice the deposit amount in statutory damages, plus the deposit itself. Small claims court is the usual route, and you don't need a lawyer. Keep your demand letter, the lease, move-out photos, and proof you returned the keys and gave a forwarding address.

turns.user: how long should the resume be with 6 years experience

turns.user: ideas to pay down 6k in card debt faster? making 85k a year, have 2 cards. what options besides just cutting spending
turns.assistant: A few options beyond cutting spending. Balance transfer card: a card with a 0 percent intro APR can give you 12 to 21 months to pay down principal, but expect a 3 to 5 percent transfer fee. Personal loan: a consolidation loan at a lower fixed rate can cut your interest, if you can qualify for a rate below your cards. Call your issuers: ask for a lower APR, since people with steady income and on-time payments sometimes get one. Hardship program: if you're struggling, ask about temporary rate reduction. Extra income: a short-term side gig or selling unused items can go straight to the balance. Pick one or two that fit your situation.

The main catches are the transfer fee, which is usually 3 to 5 percent of the amount moved, so $6,000 would cost $180 to $300 upfront. The intro rate ends after a set period, and the regular rate can be high, often over 20 percent. If you still have any balance left when it ends, you'll pay that rate on the remainder. Also, new purchases on the transfer card may not get the promo rate, and paying more than the minimum usually goes to the promo balance first. Don't use the old cards again for new spending, or you'll end up in the same spot with a bigger total.

turns.user: why does sitting hurt my lower back more than standing? shouldnt standing be worse since its more weight on the spine
turns.assistant: It's a reasonable question, but the load isn't the main issue. When you sit, your pelvis tends to tilt backward and your lower spine loses its natural curve, so the discs at the front take more pressure than they do when you stand. Sitting also keeps the back muscles in a slightly contracted, static state for a long time, which causes fatigue and stiffness. Standing keeps the spine in a more neutral position and lets the muscles move around, so it usually feels better even though you're supporting your full body weight.

turns.user: so is it the disc thing or the muscles
turns.assistant: Most of the time it's the muscles and ligaments, not the discs. Prolonged sitting makes the lower back muscles tired and tight, and the ligaments take more strain in a slumped position. The discs do bear more pressure while sitting, and that can contribute to pain if you're already sensitive, but disc problems usually come with other signs like leg pain or numbness. For general sitting-related back pain, the fix is the same either way: change position often, support the lower back, and keep moving.

turns.user: i have 300 a month i want to put into SIPs and im so lost. index fund vs active vs ELSS? im 30, planning for 15 years, and i keep reading contradictory things online
turns.assistant: Here are three realistic options for a 15-year horizon. Index fund: a low-cost fund that tracks something like the Nifty 50 or Sensex, with the lowest fees and no manager risk, but it moves with the market and won't beat it. Active fund: a fund manager picks stocks, which can outperform in some periods but often lags after fees, and you need to check the track record over at least five years. ELSS: an equity-linked savings scheme, which is an equity fund with a three-year lock-in and a tax deduction under Section 80C. For a 15-year SIP, many people start with an index fund as the core, and use an active or flexi-cap fund as a second layer. The contradictions usually come from people selling different products, so check fees and the fund's benchmark before you decide.

turns.user: what about a mix of large cap and flexi cap, whats a reasonable split
turns.assistant: A common starting point is around 60 to 70 percent in large cap and 30 to 40 percent in flexi cap. Large caps are steadier and cover the biggest companies, while flexi cap funds can move across market sizes, which can add growth but with more volatility. Since you're at 300 a month, you could do 200 in the large cap or index fund and 100 in the flexi cap. Review the mix once a year, and don't change it because of short-term swings. The split matters less than sticking to it through a bad year.
